query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of a segregating microalloying element (e.g., Nb) to the eutectic high‐entropy alloy will improve both its strength and room-temperature tensile ductility by enhancing the cohesion of internal lamellar boundaries.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventionally processed eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that form numerous internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation under room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled minor addition of a microalloying element (such as niobium) that has a strong tendency to segregate and enrich the interphase boundaries during solidification or subsequent heat treatment.
generation.conditions: The addition level must be low enough to avoid inducing unwanted brittle second phases while still promoting noticeable segregation; processing conditions (cooling rate and heat-treatment parameters) should be optimized to allow the element to diffuse to the lamellar interfaces.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced interfacial cohesion via segregation of the microalloying element at the internal boundaries, possibly forming nanoscale precipitates at the interfaces that arrest microcrack propagation.
generation.mechanism: The segregated microalloying element increases the bonding strength at the lamellar colony interfaces, reducing stress concentrations and hindering microcrack nucleation and propagation. This results in a concurrently improved capacity to absorb strain energy (better ductility) and a reinforced microstructure (higher strength).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, the modified alloy should exhibit higher yield strength and improved tensile ductility at room temperature.
generation.baseline: Conventional processing that increases strength at the expense of ductility, where brittle microcracking at internal lamellar boundaries limits ductility.
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective only if the volume fraction and distribution of the segregated element remain within a range that enhances interfacial bonding without promoting deleterious phase formation or grain coarsening.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the improvements in strength and ductility is uncertain and may depend on the choice and amount of the microalloying element, as well as the processing conditions that control its segregation behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one group of the baseline eutectic high-entropy alloy and one group with a small, controlled addition of the chosen microalloying element (e.g., Nb). Subject both groups to identical processing and heat-treatment protocols. Use electron microscopy (e.g., TEM with elemental mapping) to confirm the segregation at the lamellar boundaries. Perform standardized room-temperature tensile tests to compare yield strength and tensile ductility between the two groups.
measurements: Interface composition and precipitate distribution (using TEM/EDS or APT)
Total elongation and ductility from tensile testing
Fractography to assess microcrack initiation and propagation patterns
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified samples do not show statistically significant improvements in both yield strength and tensile ductility (or if they form brittle phases at the interfaces) compared to the baseline, the hypothesis will be falsified.
